title: Heavy strength training improves running and cycling performance following prolonged submaximal work in well-trained female athletes
authors: Vikmoen O, Rønnestad BR, Ellefsen S, Raastad T
population: 19 well-trained female duathletes (VO2max cycling 54 +/- 3, running 53 +/- 3 ml/kg/min), randomised to endurance training alone (n = 8) or endurance plus strength training (n = 11)
findings: The strength training was four lower-body exercises of 3 sets of 4-10 repetition maximum, twice a week for 11 weeks, added to normal endurance training.
The strength group raised half-squat 1RM by 45 +/- 22% and leg lean mass by 3.1 +/- 4.0%, more than the control group.

Performance in a 5-minute all-out test, taken immediately after prolonged submaximal work (3 h of cycling or 1.5 h of running), rose by 7.0 +/- 4.5% in cycling and 4.7 +/- 6.0% in running in the strength group and did not change in the control group; the running change differed between the groups.
In the strength group oxygen consumption and heart rate fell during the final 2 h of prolonged cycling, and no changes occurred during the prolonged running in either group.
limitations: Nineteen duathletes (the same sample size and group split as the 2016 trial of the same group; the abstract does not say whether the participants overlap); the outcome is a 5-minute all-out test after prolonged work, not a race; running gains had a wide spread (4.7 +/- 6.0%). Abstract read; full text not read.
implications: In women, heavy strength training improved running performance when it was tested after 1.5 hours of running, but the same group found no change in economy or a 40-minute run when tested fresh (vikmoen-2016-female-heavy-strength-running). Consistent in direction with the durability trial in men (zanini-2025-strength-economy-durability-rct), and again a small sample.
Duathletes are not runners alone; the claim is limited to 'may help late in a long effort' and is not extended to race time.
